description: We are UNSEEN, a creative team passionate about space, technology, and design. We aim to turn NASA’s Earth data into an interactive and engaging experience that makes learning about our planet fun and accessible.
summary:
Earth Jukebox turns NASA's visual data on ocean currents into sound. NASA's Earth Information Center produces powerful visualizations of our changing planet, but presenting science through sight alone excludes blind and low-vision users and can hide patterns the eye misses. Our project addresses this by pairing NASA video frames with music generated directly from the measurements inside them.

We analyzed a NASA ocean currents video frame by frame, extracting motion speed, active-area percentage, and flow direction. These values are mapped to sound: motion becomes pitch, activity becomes loudness, and direction becomes stereo position. The result is a short audio track where every change in pitch or volume reflects a real change in the ocean.

The final product is a simple, accessible website where users browse datasets, play the generated sound, watch the matching NASA frames update in sync, and read a plain-language description of what they are hearing. Earth Jukebox makes Earth science something you can listen to, not just look at.
details:
How it works:

Earth Jukebox follows a four-step pipeline. (1) A NASA video of ocean currents is split into 69 frames using OpenCV. (2) Each frame is compared to the previous one to measure motion speed, the percentage of visually active area, and the direction of flow — producing a structured dataset (JSON/CSV). (3) A Python script (NumPy, SciPy, SoundFile) maps these values to audio: motion speed controls pitch (220–880 Hz), activity controls loudness, and direction controls left/right stereo balance, producing a WAV file. (4) A lightweight website (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) plays the sound while the matching NASA frame updates in sync with playback time, so the visual and the audio move together.

Benefits and impact:

The project makes satellite Earth data accessible to blind and low-vision users, who cannot access visualization-only tools. It also gives sighted users a second way to notice patterns in the data — through sound — alongside the image. The site includes a plain-language "In words" description of the sound, labelled controls, and keyboard navigation.

Tools and languages:

Python (NumPy, OpenCV, SciPy, SoundFile) for video analysis and sound generation; HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the website; Git/GitHub for version control.

Creativity and process:

Rather than using an arbitrary or decorative soundtrack, every audible change is tied to a measured value from the NASA footage, and we deliberately avoided overstating this: the website states clearly that the audio is a sonification (a sound representation of the data), not a direct scientific measurement, and that pitch is relative to this one clip. Given a short build window, the team scoped the project to one dataset, built it completely end to end (analysis → sound → synced visuals → accessible interface), and documented clear next steps (additional NASA datasets, user-uploaded imagery) rather than leaving multiple features half-finished.
